title: Did Rochdale have any part in the Gunpowder Plot? The borough's long history with 5 November
excerpt: No record ties Rochdale to the 1605 plot, but the law that followed it shaped how the town marked 5 November for 250 years, and Cronkeyshaw has kept the bonfire tradition alive.
body:
As crowds gather on Cronkeyshaw Common tonight, a question comes round each year: did Rochdale have anything to do with the Gunpowder Plot?

The short answer is no. None of the conspirators came from Rochdale, and no historical record places the plot, or any of the men behind it, in the town. Guy Fawkes was from York, and the plotters' network was centred on the Midlands, London and Yorkshire.

Lancashire's links are real, but indirect

The wider county does have connections. Lancashire was one of the strongest Catholic areas of England at the time, and many of its gentry houses had hiding places for priests.

The most significant link runs through Lord Monteagle, the peer who received the anonymous letter of 26 October 1605 warning him to stay away from the opening of Parliament. He passed it to the government, which led to the search of the cellars beneath the House of Lords. Monteagle owned Hornby Castle in the Lune valley in north Lancashire, and his title came through his mother's family, the Stanleys.

Lancashire Museums also hold a letter written in London on 6 November 1605, the day after the plot was discovered, to William Ffarington of Worden Hall in Chorley. It describes the discovery of 36 barrels of gunpowder beneath the Parliament house, showing how quickly news reached the county.

Closer to home, Ordsall Hall in Salford is often said to be where the plot was hatched. That story comes from William Harrison Ainsworth's 1841 novel Guy Fawkes. Historians at the Gunpowder Plot Society have found no evidence for it and describe the claim as false.

How the plot shaped 5 November in Rochdale

The plot's lasting mark on Rochdale came from the law that followed it. The Observance of 5th November Act, passed in May 1606, required every Church of England parish to hold an annual thanksgiving service on 5 November and to read the act aloud. That would have included Rochdale's parish church, St Chad's. The requirement stayed in force until Parliament repealed it in 1859.

By then, bonfires and fireworks had long since become the popular side of the day, and that is the tradition that survives.

Cronkeyshaw's bonfire

In modern times, Cronkeyshaw Common has been the focus of Rochdale's celebrations. The council-run bonfire and fireworks there draw hundreds, and in some years thousands, of people.

It has not always been secure. In 2008, the town centre funfair and fireworks were cancelled because the organisers could not fund them. Later that year, a council report proposed ending large events on the common altogether, citing damage to the land, the lack of parking and the effect on nearby streets. Fairs and circuses had used the common for more than 30 years by then.

The bonfire survived. In 2013, thousands turned out despite torrential rain that left the common deep in mud. This year, the display has been changed to reduced-noise fireworks set to music.

The council has also banned unauthorised bonfires on its own land since 2011, steering celebrations towards organised displays.

So while Rochdale played no part in the events of 1605, it has spent more than four centuries marking them, first in church and now on Cronkeyshaw Common.

Do you have memories or photographs of bonfire nights in Rochdale from years gone by? Share them with us in the comments.
